content:
The ASUS ProArt PA27UCGE is a 27-inch 4K monitor with several standout features in the competitive display market. First, it supports a high refresh rate of up to 160Hz, handling smooth web scrolling, gaming, and video editing with ease. It also comes with an optional monitor hood to reduce ambient light interference and features a built-in motorized calibrator for periodic color calibration.

We previously reviewed ASUS's 5K ProArt (review) and 6K ProArt displays (review), both of which are exceptional value third-party options for Mac users. How does this ProArt display, which adds several extra features but at a lower resolution, perform? Watch our video review for details.

The ASUS ProArt display line has always focused on photo editing and video production, and this 27-inch 4K PA27UCGE is no exception. While it cannot deliver the rich, deep blacks of OLED technology, its 600-nit IPS panel provides excellent contrast and sustained brightness, making it well-suited for working in environments where lighting cannot be fully controlled.

Video: ASUS 4K 160Hz Monitor—Is It Worth Buying?

The PA27UCGE supports variable refresh rates up to 160Hz at 4K resolution. This not only makes text scrolling smoother but is also ideal for high-frame-rate video production and gaming. I tested it alongside a 16-inch MacBook Pro with 120Hz ProMotion, and it's a pleasure to have both screens with matching refresh rates. Even with just the M4 Mac mini connected to a single display, the support for 120Hz, 144Hz, or even 160Hz is highly practical.

While I always prefer glossy displays over matte coatings, this monitor's anti-glare, low-reflectance "LuxPixel" coating effectively reduces reflections while maintaining text clarity, without the text blur commonly seen on typical matte displays. It's worth noting that text sharpness is still somewhat affected, but this is the best-performing matte display I've used—second only to screens featuring nano-etch technology like Apple's matte option.

The PA27UCGE also includes an optional monitor hood to help block ambient light reflections. I found installing the hood somewhat cumbersome, and the design and build quality feel a bit clumsy, but once installed, it effectively blocks ambient light from hitting the display surface.

macOS Scaling

One drawback of using a 4K display with macOS is the inability to achieve perfect native 1:1 scaling at the HiDPI 2880×1440 resolution, which most users desire at this screen size. Like all 4K displays on macOS, setting the display to 2560×1440 causes the system to first render at a virtual 5120×2880 canvas, then apply fractional scaling down to a pixel-doubled 1440p "retina" HiDPI resolution. While the result closely approximates a true 5K panel, text sharpness suffers slightly because it is not perfect 1:1 scaling.

Using the native pixel-doubled 1920×1080 resolution provides true 1:1 scaling and razor-sharp text, but at the cost of significantly reduced workspace. For most people, sacrificing a bit of sharpness for more screen space is an easy trade-off, but it's worth noting. When my eyesight was better, I was more bothered by this issue, but as I've gotten older, such differences have become easier to accept.

Color Calibration Measurements

A motorized calibrator is built into the bottom bezel beneath the logo, allowing the ProArt 4K to self-calibrate without the need for external calibration tools or software, resulting in more accurate color. That said, I still prefer using an external tool like the Calibrite Display Pro HL for greater flexibility.

The built-in motorized calibrator can be used via the OSD for calibration, but to view actual data, you'll need to install the Asus ProArt Calibration tool. The fixed position of the built-in calibrator is one limitation, but its biggest advantage is the ability to schedule automatic calibrations when the display is idle. Since calibration can take over 30 minutes, this feature is highly useful in the long run.

According to the included calibration report, this unit has a Delta-E sRGB average of 0.78 and a DCI-P3 average of 1.12—both excellent figures. This rating measures the difference between the original input color and what the screen actually displays, so lower values indicate higher color accuracy. In my experience, values below 2 are considered ideal.

ASUS claims the PA27UCGE offers 98% DCI-P3 color gamut coverage, making it ideal for color grading and video editing in Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve. To verify ASUS's claims, I tested using both the built-in calibrator and the Calibrate Display Pro HL, paired with Calibrate's Profiler software and ASUS's own ProArt calibration tool.

Measurements showed a DCI-P3 Delta E average of less than 1.2, closely matching ASUS's claimed figures. DCI-P3 color gamut coverage was also quite accurate. When editing and color grading Canon Log 2 footage shot on a Canon R5 Mark II in Final Cut Pro, overall colors were largely accurate.

More importantly, the display's color and brightness uniformity performed well, with brightness tolerance staying below 5 in nearly all Calibrite Profiler tests. For brightness, ASUS rates it at 600 nits, but I measured over 700 nits at peak during testing.

Design, Build Quality, and Ergonomics

The ASUS ProArt 4K display follows ASUS's typical design language, and like the previous 5K and 6K ProArt displays, its build quality is unlikely to win awards. This doesn't mean ASUS's build quality is poor—rather, Apple invests heavily in this area, so its displays almost always feature higher manufacturing standards.

Third-party display manufacturers typically don't compete with Apple in this regard. Instead, they generally offer better value with more affordable, plastic-heavy enclosures that are easier to mass-produce.

In short, of course I'd prefer an ASUS monitor with a unibody aluminum chassis and smooth, well-balanced adjustments, but the reality is that finding a third-party display manufacturer willing to go head-to-head with Apple in this area is difficult. ASUS compensates with a richer overall feature set, higher refresh rates, and more I/O options.

Ergonomics

From an ergonomic standpoint, the ASUS ProArt 4K offers fairly comprehensive adjustments. The monitor tilts +23 or -5 degrees, swivels 90 degrees left and right, pivots ±30 degrees horizontally, and provides 120mm of height adjustment. The smoothness and balance of adjustments don't match the Apple Studio Display. Apple offers tilt adjustment on the base Studio Display, while the tilt- and height-adjustable stand costs an extra $200, but it completely lacks swivel and pivot functions.

Overall, the ASUS PA27UCGE leans more toward practical than aesthetic in design, build quality, and ergonomics. Of course, I'd love a clean, logo- and button-free front bezel like the Studio Display, but considering this 4K display from ASUS is only $800, its value is undeniable.

Ports

While Apple added Thunderbolt 5 daisy-chaining to the new Studio Display, third-party displays like the PA27UCGE offer a richer selection of connectivity options.

The USB 3.2 Gen 1 upstream port is the primary interface most Mac users will use to connect a MacBook or Mac mini. For laptop users, the USB upstream port can deliver up to 96W of power, enough to fully charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro. The PA27UCGE also features dual HDMI 2.1 ports and a DisplayPort 1.4 input, suitable for connecting PCs, gaming consoles, or set-top boxes like Apple TV.

  • Digital Inputs: 1 x DisplayPort v1.4 2 x HDMI 2.1 1 x DisplayPort over USB Type-C
  • USB Ports: 1 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 Upstream Type-C (Data Only) 1 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 Downstream Type-C 2 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 Downstream Type-A
  • Audio: Headphone Jack Built-in Speakers (2W x 2)

In addition to the built-in USB hub, the display also supports automatic KVM functionality, allowing you to easily connect two computers simultaneously and share a single mouse and keyboard.

9to5Mac's Take

The ASUS ProArt PA27UCGE offers exceptional value for its price. It features excellent DCI-P3 color gamut support, making it ideal for photo and video editing, and offers a high refresh rate that pairs perfectly with a ProMotion-equipped MacBook Pro.

The LuxPixel matte display reduces reflections without overly compromising text clarity, and while the included monitor hood isn't elegantly designed, it effectively blocks ambient light.

Not to be overlooked, this display provides extensive input support, including dual HDMI, DisplayPort, and USB-C, along with hub and KVM functionality.

Like most third-party displays on the market, its build quality can't match Apple's own displays, but this is true of nearly all third-party products. As compensation, it offers far richer ergonomic adjustments than Apple.

ASUS provides a 3-year warranty for ProArt displays (including the PA27UCGE), with a free 2-year extension upon registration, for a total of 5 years of coverage. Considering that most displays on the market (including Apple's) only offer a 1-year warranty, 5 years of coverage is highly appealing.

It's certainly not perfect, but at $800, this ASUS ProArt 4K display significantly outperforms its price point. For video editors or gamers seeking a high-refresh-rate external display, I absolutely recommend it.
